newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shares end firm as dollar support holds.
newsitem.headline: German shares end firm as dollar support holds.

text.p: German blue chip shares posted modest gains on Thursday as the firm dollar and selective interest in chemical and engineering shares helped the market hit fresh record highs in late trading.
The IBIS DAX index, amid what dealers said were ample trading volumes, rose 10.05 points to end the screen-based trading session at 3,124.78 points, just off a new alltime high of 3,125.70.
That was some 20 points above the DAX's mid-afternoon bourse session at 3,104.14 points.
"There is no concerted push upward but the dollar is still over 1.65 and that is still a positive," one dealer noted.
"With people constantly taking up chances to come into the market, I think we are O.K. at these levels," said another, adding that he saw 3,150 points as an attainable short-term goal for the DAX.

The dollar -- a crucial factor for German exporters' income -- was buoyed all day after a report showing a sharp rise in German jobless data in January, when unemployment hit 4.66 million, the highest level since the 1930s.

The chemical sector was ahead for the second day in a row, with the DAX-100 chemical sector index up 0.6 percent, rising three times faster than the top 100 shares. Dealers say chemicals are catching up now after lagging the DAX for months.

The engineering sector was even more in demand after better-than-expected year-end earnings from Preussag AG and a decision to hold its dividend at 12 marks, countering some market fears that the payout would be cut.
After an initial surge flagged as bourse trading continued, Preussag ended floor dealings up three marks at 391, later regaining ground to close IBIS dealings at 395.10.

Engineering group Mannesmann rose 14.50 marks to 658 in bourse trading and ended the day at 661 after Merrill Lynch raised the stock to a "buy" from "neutral" and, according to dealers, raised its target price for the stock significantly.

Software group SAP's preferred shares slipped 4.70 marks to 249.80 after a placement at 244 marks of some 3.54 million common shares once held by SAP's co-founder Hans-Werner Hector, who resigned in late 1996.
The shares pared their losses in later IBIS trade to 251.10 marks.
The Bundesbank's largely-expected decision to leave interest rates unchanged had minimal impact on the market.
Dealers generally see no immediate impetus for a move on rates and one noted: "With this kind of jobless rate, we can more or less rule out a rate hike."
